It does not smuggle induction because it relies on the logical content of tests passed, not an assumption that the future will resemble the past.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If Popper's formal definition of verisimilitude is logically incoherent (as critics like Miller and Tich\u00fd argued).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If acting on a theory necessarily implies an expectation of its future success, which is inductive.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'severity' of tests cannot be defined without assuming some regularity in nature.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper distinguishes between 'probability' (inductive support) and 'verisimilitude' (closeness to truth). A theory with higher corroboration has survived more severe tests, implying it has higher verisimilitude. The preference is a rational choice to act on the theory closest to truth, acknowledging it may still be false.
